idiom_name: sealed interface + one record per state whose methods return the next state type
implementation_notes: Modern Java encodes states as a sealed interface with one record per state: state-specific methods are declared only on the record that owns the transition and return the next record, while a shared parent interface carries the operations valid everywhere, and switch pattern matching (Java 21) narrows a state whose kind is unknown. Type erasure does not prevent compile-time state tracking - the type argument is checked before erasure - so bounded generic staging works too, but Java has no consume-on-transition and no standard-library protocol support. JATYC, an external Checker Framework plugin, is the only tool that additionally checks call sequences and protocol completion.
pitfalls: Records are reference values: every alias keeps its own state, so a disconnected reference and a connected reference to 'the same' resource can coexist unless the object is the sole owner.
Any state-specific method leaked onto the shared parent interface re-opens the invalid call; the parent must contain only always-valid operations.
Exhaustive narrowing requires Java 21 switch patterns; on older releases a switch needs a default branch and the exhaustiveness guarantee is lost.
